books.blurb: Eric Jorgenson gathered years of Naval Ravikant's tweets, podcast conversations and essays and organized them into one short guide. Naval is an entrepreneur and investor best known for cofounding AngelList. The book has two halves. The first is about wealth. Naval argues that getting rich is a learnable skill, not luck. It comes from owning assets, building specific knowledge that others can't easily copy, using leverage like code and media, and taking accountability for your work. The second half is about happiness. Naval treats happiness as a skill too, built through habits like meditation, reading, exercise and letting go of endless desire. The thread connecting both halves is freedom. Wealth buys freedom from having to work. Inner peace frees you from your own restless mind.

lessons.t: Getting rich is a skill, not luck
lessons.b: Seek wealth, meaning assets that earn while you sleep, rather than chasing a salary or status, because wealth creation is a positive-sum game anyone can learn.
Your edge is knowledge that can't be taught in a classroom, found by following your genuine curiosity toward work that feels like play to you but looks like work to others.

lessons.t: Use leverage that needs no permission
lessons.b: Code and media multiply your effort without anyone's permission, letting one person's work reach millions while they sleep.
Putting your name on your work and owning the results earns trust and rewards, and with leverage, good judgment becomes the most valuable skill you can have.

lessons.t: Play long-term games with long-term people
lessons.b: The biggest returns in money, relationships and reputation come from compounding over years with people you trust.

lessons.t: Happiness is a skill you can train
lessons.b: Happiness is mostly a state of peace you can cultivate, and every desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get it.

lessons.t: Wealth and peace both buy freedom
lessons.b: Productize yourself to earn freedom from forced work, and build habits like meditation, reading and exercise to earn freedom from your own restless mind.

books.title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
books.author: Mark Manson
books.blurb: Mark Manson argues that modern self-help has it backwards. Constantly chasing positivity and success only reminds us of what we lack. He says we all have a limited amount of attention and concern, so the real skill is choosing carefully what deserves it. Life will always bring problems. Happiness comes from picking good problems and enjoying the work of solving them. Manson takes aim at entitlement, the belief that we are special and deserve to feel good all the time. He urges us to adopt better values, take responsibility for everything in our lives even when it isn't our fault, doubt our own certainty, and treat failure as the path to growth. Finally, he argues that facing our own mortality helps us see clearly what is truly worth caring about.

lessons.t: Chasing Happiness Makes You Less Happy
lessons.b: Wanting a positive experience is itself a negative experience, so accepting the negative is what actually frees you.

lessons.t: Choose Your Problems, Not Problem-Free Life
lessons.b: Life is never free of problems, so happiness comes from choosing struggles you enjoy and solving them.
Believing you are exceptional, whether great or uniquely broken, is entitlement that stops you from growing.

lessons.t: Pick Better Values to Measure Yourself
lessons.b: Your suffering depends on your values, so trade shallow ones like pleasure and popularity for ones you control, like honesty and growth.

lessons.t: Responsibility Is Not the Same as Fault
lessons.b: Even when something isn't your fault, you are always responsible for how you respond to it.
Action creates motivation, so doing something small, even badly, beats waiting to feel ready.
Committing to a few things by rejecting the rest, and remembering life is short, shows what is truly worth caring about.

books.title: Four Thousand Weeks
books.author: Oliver Burkeman
books.blurb: Oliver Burkeman, a former productivity enthusiast, argues that most time management advice rests on an impossible promise: that with enough efficiency, we can finally get on top of everything. The average human life lasts only about four thousand weeks, and no system can make that enough for all our ambitions. Worse, becoming more efficient often just brings more demands. Drawing on philosophy and psychology, Burkeman suggests a different path: accept your limits, make hard choices about what to neglect, and stop treating the present as a mere stepping stone to some future moment of control. He explores why we flee into distraction, why patience is a superpower, why rest needs no justification, and why time is richer when shared with others. The result is a liberating, deeply humane guide to spending a finite life well.

lessons.t: You Only Get Four Thousand Weeks
lessons.b: An average life lasts about four thousand weeks, and facing that limit honestly is the starting point for using time well.
Getting through tasks faster rarely frees you, because doing more usually just attracts more to do, like an inbox that refills as you empty it.
Since you can never do everything, the real skill is deliberately deciding which important things you will fail at so you can focus on what matters most.
Distraction is often an escape from the discomfort of facing hard, limited, uncertain work, so the cure is accepting that discomfort rather than relying only on willpower or apps.
Treating every moment as a means to some future payoff robs you of life now, so value activities like rest and hobbies for their own sake.
Meaningful work and change unfold at their own pace, so staying with something through its slow, unoriginal early stages is what eventually leads somewhere distinctive.
Accepting that your life is tiny on a cosmic scale, and that time is best shared with others, frees you from impossible standards to do modest things that truly matter.
